prompt: Which of the four parts of a server does a managed service keep out of your reach entirely?
hint: Think about what needs a shell on the machine.

choices.text: The roles and grants
choices.why: Those live inside the database, and they stay yours wherever the server runs.

choices.text: The schema of your tables
choices.why: The schema is yours in every column of the table: the provider never decides what your tables are.

choices.text: Your SQL queries
choices.why: You connect with the same psql and send the same SQL. That part does not change.

choices.text: The data files
choices.why: Right. With no shell there is no data directory to look at; only the provider sees the files.

prompt: A team runs PostgreSQL in a container and leaves out the `-v` option. What happens to the data when the container is removed?
hint: Where does the data directory live without a volume?

choices.text: Docker moves it to a default volume
choices.why: There is no default volume that outlives the container in this case: the files were inside it.

choices.text: It goes with the container
choices.why: Right. Without a volume the data directory is part of the container's own filesystem.

choices.text: The server refuses to start until a volume is given
choices.why: The image refuses to start without a password, not without a volume. It starts happily and loses the data later.

choices.text: It stays on the host under /var/lib/postgresql
choices.why: That path is inside the container. The host's /var/lib/postgresql belongs to a packaged server, if there is one.

prompt: Which of these remain your job on a managed service? Choose all that apply.
hint: What lives inside the database, and what is a decision rather than a chore?

choices.text: Granting a reporting role read access to two schemas
choices.why: Yes. Roles and grants are inside the database, wherever it runs.

choices.text: Noticing that one large table needs different autovacuum thresholds
choices.why: Yes. The provider runs autovacuum; it does not know your tables.

choices.text: Installing the operating system's security updates
choices.why: That is the provider's, along with the rest of the machine.

choices.text: Choosing when to move to the next major version
choices.why: Yes. The console executes the upgrade; the decision and the testing are yours.

choices.text: Reading postgresql.conf on the server
choices.why: There is no shell and no file to read. Parameters are a form in the console.

prompt: Match each way of having a server to where its log goes.
hint: One writes a file, one writes to its output, one keeps it for you.

pairs.right: The container's output, kept by Docker
The provider's console, or a download

prompt: Why does the course recommend a virtual machine over installing PostgreSQL on the laptop you work on, even when the laptop runs Ubuntu?
hint: Think about lesson 9.

choices.text: PostgreSQL runs faster in a virtual machine
choices.why: It runs slightly slower, if anything. Speed is not the argument.

choices.text: Ubuntu's packages only install inside a virtual machine
choices.why: They install on any Ubuntu, and the course says the installed path works as printed.

choices.text: Its breakages stay away from your own files
choices.why: Right. Filling a disk is a lesson in a virtual machine and an afternoon lost on a laptop.

choices.text: A licence restricts PostgreSQL on personal computers
choices.why: PostgreSQL's licence allows any use. Nothing restricts where it runs.

prompt: A student follows the course on Postgres.app on macOS. Which kind of lesson will match their screen?
hint: PostgreSQL is the same program; what is around it is not.

choices.text: Lessons done inside psql
choices.why: Right. Inside the server everything is the same; around it nothing is.

choices.text: Lessons about where the files live
choices.why: The paths are exactly what differs between installers.

choices.text: Lessons about systemd and the service
choices.why: macOS has no systemd. The service starts another way.

choices.text: None, because macOS cannot run PostgreSQL 16
choices.why: It runs it fine. Postgres.app and Homebrew both install 16.

prompt: How many gigabytes of memory does the course recommend giving the virtual machine?
hint: Twice what a lighter course would ask.

prompt: In `psql (PostgreSQL) 16.15`, what does the 15 tell you?
hint: Two numbers, two kinds of release.

choices.text: Ubuntu's fifteenth rebuild of the package
choices.why: Ubuntu's own version is the part in brackets, 0ubuntu0.24.04.1.

choices.text: A minor release: fixes only
choices.why: Right. Lesson 20 relies on that difference.

choices.text: The fifteenth major version since 16 began
choices.why: The major version is the first number alone. Since version 10 it has one part.

choices.text: The number of clusters the package can run
choices.why: A version string says nothing about clusters.

prompt: On Ubuntu, the systemd unit of the cluster called main of version 16 is postgresql@___.
hint: Version, a dash, name.

prompt: `pg_lsclusters` prints one row per cluster. Which program is it part of?
hint: It is not in the PostgreSQL source.

choices.text: psql, as a backslash command
choices.why: psql's own commands start with a backslash and run inside psql. This one runs in the shell.

choices.text: postgresql-common
choices.why: Right. It is also what lets several versions run on one machine.

choices.text: systemd
choices.why: systemd knows units, not data directories or ports.

choices.text: The PostgreSQL server itself
choices.why: Upstream PostgreSQL has no notion of several clusters on a machine.

prompt: Right after installing, `psql` answers `role "ana" does not exist`. What is missing?
hint: The server answered. It just does not know the name.

choices.text: The operating-system user ana
choices.why: That user exists: it is the one typing. The server keeps its own list.

choices.text: A running server
choices.why: A FATAL message means something answered. A stopped server answers nothing.

choices.text: A database role called ana
choices.why: Right. `createuser` makes one.

choices.text: A password for the role postgres
choices.why: Nothing asked about postgres, and over the socket no password is used.

prompt: Why does `psql -U postgres`, typed as ana, fail with `Peer authentication failed`, while `sudo -u postgres psql` works?
hint: Peer means the two names have to agree.

choices.text: Over the socket a role is allowed only to the operating-system user of the same name
choices.why: Right. sudo makes you that user; -U only asks for the role.

choices.text: The postgres role has a password that ana does not know, and sudo supplies it for her
choices.why: Peer authentication never asks for a password. It compares names.

choices.text: Only root may connect as postgres
choices.why: root would be refused the same way: root is not called postgres either.

choices.text: -U is not a valid option of psql
choices.why: It is valid, and it works wherever the authentication rule allows it.

prompt: In the course's psql, the prompt reads `ana=#`. What would an ordinary role see at the end instead of `#`?
hint: A character that is also a shell's.

choices.why: That is the operating system's ordinary-user prompt, not psql's.
A dash appears when psql waits for the rest of a statement, as in `ana-#`.
psql does not use it in its default prompt.
Right. `#` marks a superuser.

prompt: `psql -h localhost` asks ana for a password, and plain `psql` does not. Both reach the same server. What explains it?
hint: Two doors, two rules.

choices.text: localhost is treated as a remote machine and remote roles always need passwords
choices.why: It is the same machine; what differs is that the connection used TCP, and the TCP rule asks for a password.

choices.text: The server forgets the role between connections
choices.why: Roles are stored in the cluster and persist.

choices.text: ana's role was created only for the socket
choices.why: A role is not tied to a door. The rules for each door are separate from the role.

choices.text: TCP is matched by another line of the rules, one that wants a password
choices.why: Right. The socket line says peer, the TCP line says password, and both come from pg_hba.conf.

prompt: In the official postgres:16 container, where is postgresql.conf?
hint: It is PostgreSQL's own default, not Ubuntu's.

choices.text: In /etc/postgresql/16/main
choices.why: That is the Debian and Ubuntu package's choice.

choices.text: Nowhere: containers are configured only with -c arguments
choices.why: The file exists; -c arguments override it.

choices.text: Inside the data directory, and so inside the volume
choices.why: Right. /var/lib/postgresql/data/postgresql.conf, as SHOW config_file printed.

choices.text: In Docker's own configuration
choices.why: Docker knows nothing about PostgreSQL's settings.

prompt: A developer moves a container from postgres:16 to postgres:17 and keeps the same volume. What should they expect?
hint: The image changed; the files in the volume did not.

choices.text: The new server refuses to start on a data directory from version 16
choices.why: Right. A major upgrade moves the data, not just the image.

choices.text: The new server upgrades the old files on its first start, then runs as before
choices.why: No server converts a previous major version's files by itself. That is lesson 20's whole problem.

choices.text: It works, because the data format is the same in every version
choices.why: The format changes between major versions; that is what makes them major.

choices.text: Docker refuses to mount a volume created by another image
choices.why: Docker mounts it happily. It is PostgreSQL that refuses.

prompt: On a managed service, your first role belongs to something like rds_superuser. What is it missing compared with a real superuser?
hint: The provider must keep the machine to itself.

choices.text: The right to create tables
choices.why: It creates tables, roles and databases.

choices.text: The right to connect over the network
choices.why: Network is the only way in, and it works.

choices.text: Reaching the operating system
choices.why: Right. That is the line the provider holds.

choices.text: The right to grant privileges to other roles
choices.why: It grants freely inside its databases.

prompt: A provider upgrades minor versions automatically. Which part of an upgrade is still left for you to do?
hint: Minor and major are not the same job.

choices.text: Reading the major release notes and testing
choices.why: Right. The console executes; it does not decide or test for you.

choices.text: Compiling the new minor version
choices.why: Nobody compiles anything; the provider ships binaries.

choices.text: Copying the data files to the new machine
choices.why: You never see the files on a managed service.

choices.text: Restarting the instance after each minor upgrade
choices.why: The provider restarts it as part of the upgrade.

prompt: `psql` answers `No such file or directory` and `Is the server running locally`. What is the first thing to run?
hint: No FATAL means nothing answered.

choices.text: `sudo -u postgres createuser --superuser $USER`
choices.why: That fixes a missing role, which is a FATAL message from a running server.

choices.text: `sudo apt install -y postgresql` again
choices.why: psql ran, so the client is installed. The server is what is not answering.

choices.text: `pg_lsclusters`
choices.why: Right. The socket exists only while the server runs.

choices.text: `sudo rm /var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432`
choices.why: The file is not there, which is exactly the complaint. Deleting is never the step.

prompt: A cluster will not start after somebody edited its configuration. Where does the reason appear first?
hint: The last column of pg_lsclusters.

choices.text: In the cluster's log
choices.why: Right. The last lines name the bad setting.

choices.text: In psql's error message
choices.why: psql only learns that nothing is listening.

choices.text: In /etc/postgresql/16/main/postgresql.conf itself
choices.why: The file holds the mistake, not a message about it.

choices.text: In the hypervisor's window
choices.why: The hypervisor knows nothing about PostgreSQL.

prompt: VirtualBox refuses to start the machine and mentions VT-x. What does that mean?
hint: The processor can; something is stopping it.

choices.text: The Ubuntu image is damaged
choices.why: The machine never got as far as reading the image.

choices.text: The computer is too old to run a virtual machine
choices.why: Almost every processor of the last decade has the feature. It is usually switched off.

choices.text: Virtualisation is off in the firmware
choices.why: Right. A BIOS or UEFI setting, or Hyper-V on Windows.

choices.text: The machine was given too little memory
choices.why: Too little memory makes it slow, not refused.

prompt: Put the steps from a fresh Ubuntu server to `ana=#` in order.
hint: Install, then the role, then the database, then connect.
trap: createdb before createuser fails: the server does not know who is asking.

prompt: Match each message to its cause.
hint: Read the part after FATAL, or notice there is none.

pairs.right: asking for a role that is not your name

prompt: A colleague's server has two rows in `pg_lsclusters`: `16 main 5432 online` and `16 test 5433 online`. How many postmaster processes does the machine run?
hint: One cluster, one server.

choices.text: One, serving both clusters
choices.why: A postmaster serves exactly one data directory.

choices.text: Two, one for each cluster, on different ports
choices.why: Right. Each cluster is a whole server with its own processes.

choices.text: None until somebody connects
choices.why: online means the postmaster is running and listening.

choices.text: Two, but only one of them can be online at any given moment
choices.why: Both say online; different ports let them coexist.

prompt: You need the `postgres` role on the course's server for one command. Which way works without changing any configuration?
hint: Become the user whose name matches.

choices.text: psql -U postgres
choices.why: Peer authentication refuses it: you are not the user postgres.

choices.text: sudo -u postgres psql
choices.why: Right. You become the operating-system user, and peer lets that user in as the role.

choices.text: psql -h localhost -U postgres
choices.why: Over TCP it asks for a password, and the postgres role has none.

choices.text: sudo psql
choices.why: That runs psql as root, and there is no role called root.

prompt: PostgreSQL's word for one running server and the directory its data lives in is a ___.
hint: An older sense of a word that now means many machines.
